questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Period of a low circular orbit
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the period of a low circular orbit from radius and speed
questions.stem: Tank log, 12 March: the debris-tracking satellite orbits at radius 7.0e6 m with speed 7.5e3 m per s. What is its orbital period in minutes?
questions.explanation: The period is the circumference divided by the speed: 2 pi times 7.0e6 over 7.5e3 gives 5864 s, or 97.7 minutes. Using the radius rather than the circumference would give a smaller value.
questions.hint: Period is the orbit circumference over the speed.

options.text: Escape speed is the speed at which a body on the surface can leave the planet and never return.
Escape speed is the speed needed to orbit just above the surface without falling in.
options.misconception: confuses escape speed with the circular orbital speed

options.text: Escape speed depends on the mass of the escaping body, so a heavy tag needs more speed.

options.text: Escape speed is fixed by the radius of the planet alone and does not depend on its mass.
options.misconception: thinks escape speed is set by the radius alone

questions.explanation: Escape speed follows from the square root of 2 G M over R, and it is the speed at which the planet's pull can no longer bend the path back to the surface. Option B gives the circular orbital speed instead.

options.text: The planet's pull always points along the radius, so it exerts no torque about the planet's centre.

answer.exemplar: Write down that the upward reactions at the two supports must add up to the total weight of the beam plus any extra load on it. questions.topic: Why a circular orbit is a constant-angular-momentum orbit
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a central pull keeps orbital angular momentum constant
questions.stem: Written explanation in the log of why the plastic tag's orbital angular momentum never changes along its circular path.

answer.exemplar: The tag is held in its circular path by the planet's gravitational pull, which always points straight at the centre of the planet. Angular momentum about that centre can only change if a torque acts about it, and a pull whose line of action passes through the centre produces no torque at all. The tag's speed and radius therefore stay constant too, and the product of them, which is the angular momentum per unit mass, is the same at every point of the orbit.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that the central pull exerts no torque about the planet's centre, so angular momentum is constant, and notes the perpendicular radius. A poor answer mentions only the constant speed.
questions.hint: Constant angular momentum needs no torque about the centre.

questions.stem: The escape speed for a planet with G M of 3.986e14 and radius 6.37e6 m. What is the escape speed at the surface?
questions.explanation: Escape speed is the root of 2 G M over R, so 2 times 3.986e14 over 6.37e6 gives 1.2515e8, whose root is 11187 m per s. Using G M over R gives the orbital speed.
questions.hint: Escape speed is the root of 2 G M over R.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a circular orbit is a constant-angular-momentum orbit
questions.learningObjective: Find an angular speed from angular momentum and moment of inertia
questions.stem: On the bench model the orbiting satellite has an angular momentum of 2.16 kg m squared per s and a moment of inertia of 0.72 kg m squared about the model's axis. What is its angular speed?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum equals moment of inertia times angular speed, so the angular speed is 2.16 divided by 0.72, which is 3.0 rad per s. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 1.56.
questions.hint: Angular speed is angular momentum over inertia.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Rate at which a gyroscope sweeps round under a turning torque
questions.learningObjective: Compare the gyroscope response with and without its spin
questions.stem: Two stages with the ship's gyroscope: first a sideways push while the wheel spins fast, then the same push with the wheel at rest.

options.text: Both stages give the same small sweep, because the response depends only on the size of the push.
options.misconception: claims both stages give the same response

options.text: The spinning wheel sweeps about the vertical, while the wheel at rest simply tips over in the push direction.
The stationary wheel also sweeps about the vertical, though more slowly, because the push is the same.
options.misconception: claims the stationary wheel sweeps as well

options.text: Both stages tip the wheel in the direction of the push, because a push always acts on the axle.
options.misconception: claims the spinning wheel tips like a still one

questions.explanation: Precession needs the wheel's own angular momentum, so a spinning wheel sweeps about the vertical while a stationary wheel merely tips. Option A ignores the spin entirely.
questions.hint: The spin is what changes the response to a push.
